blocks.text:
# Week 6, Day 3.1 - Prerequisites check

**No new TypeScript today.** Git is a tool, not a language feature - so this file is short.

| In play | Taught in |
|---|---|
| `async` / `await`, Promises | [week3/day3_1](/learn/w3/d3/p1) |
| Template literals | no formal primer yet - short recap below |
| Arrays of objects | [week3/day5_1](/learn/w3/d5/p1) |
| `for...of` | [week4/day4_1](/learn/w4/d4/p1) |

One new API - and it is not Playwright.

**Next:** [Day 3.2 - Git, for people who write tests](/learn/w6/d3/p2)

## Recap - template literals

You have been reading these since your very first spec without a formal introduction, and today's
cells are full of them. Backticks instead of quotes, and `${...}` drops a value in:

| Written | Produces |
|---|---|
| `` `git version` `` | `git version` |
| `` `${REPO_ROOT}/package.json` `` | the path, with the variable substituted |
| `"${REPO_ROOT}/x"` | the literal text `${REPO_ROOT}/x` - **quotes do not substitute** |

That third row is the mistake to avoid: `${}` only means anything inside backticks.

// Your turn — retype the example above from memory, then run it.
// Typing beats reading. Peek above if you get stuck.

## `Deno.Command` - running a program from a cell

Every Git command in [day3_2](/learn/w6/d3/p2) really runs. This is the mechanism: it starts a
program, waits, and hands back what it printed.

| Piece | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `new Deno.Command("git", { args: [...] })` | the program and its arguments, **not** a shell string |
| `cwd` | which folder to run in - decisive for git |
| `stdout: "piped"` | capture the output instead of letting it vanish |
| `await p.output()` | run it, wait, get `{ code, stdout, stderr }` |
| `code` | **0 means success.** Every CI tool on earth reads this |

Arguments are an array, so nothing is word-split or glob-expanded - a path with a space works.

// Your turn — retype the example above from memory, then run it.
// Typing beats reading. Peek above if you get stuck.

## Exit codes are the whole CI contract

A test run that exits `0` is a green build. Anything else is red. That is all Jenkins, GitHub
Actions and Azure ever check - worth internalising now, because Days 4 and 5 are built on it.

// Your turn — retype the example above from memory, then run it.
// Typing beats reading. Peek above if you get stuck.
**Next:** [Day 3.2 - Git, for people who write tests](/learn/w6/d3/p2)

blocks.text:
# Week 6, Day 3.2 - Git, for people who write tests

Until now your tests have lived on your machine. That is fine until the day someone else needs
them, or a CI server does - and a CI server can only run code it can **fetch**.

By the end of this lesson you will have watched a repository get created, committed, pushed,
pulled, and a push **rejected** - all for real, in a temp folder.

> **Mode: Deno.** No Playwright here. These cells run `git`.

## Why a tester needs this at all

| Without a shared repo | With one |
|---|---|
| Your tests exist on one laptop | anyone can fetch them |
| A teammate off sick blocks the suite | their work is already pushed |
| Jenkins cannot reach your code | it clones a URL |
| A dead disk loses the work | history is on the server |

GitHub's job in one line: **one agreed copy of the code that is not on anybody's laptop.**

## The two words

| Word | Direction |
|---|---|
| **push** | my commits → the server |
| **pull** | the server's commits → me |

And the rule that prevents most Git pain: **pull before you push.** Step 11 below shows what
happens when you do not.

## The commands, in order

| # | Command | Job |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | `git init` | turn a folder into a repository |
| 2 | `git remote add origin <url>` | tell it where the server is |
| 3 | `git status` | what has changed, what is tracked |
| 4 | `git add -A` | stage everything for the next commit |
| 5 | `git commit -m "message"` | save a snapshot, with a reason |
| 6 | `git push -u origin master` | send it |
| 7 | `git pull origin master` | collect what others sent |

Three states, which is the part people find confusing:

| State | `git status` shows | Means |
|---|---|---|
| untracked / modified | `??` or ` M` | git is not storing this yet |
| staged | `A` or `M` | will be in the next commit |
| committed | nothing | saved locally - **still not on the server** |

Committed is not pushed. That trips up everyone once.

## Now watch it happen

The script below builds a throwaway repo **and a second one that acts as GitHub**, so push and
pull are real rather than described.

> **Safe:** it works in a temp folder and deletes it afterwards. It never touches this project or
> its remote.

## What that output proved

| Step | Watch for |
|---|---|
| 4 | `??` - git can see the files and is not storing them |
| 5 | `A` - now staged |
| 7 | `master -> master` - the commit reaches the remote |
| 9 → 10 | the teammate's file is **absent**, then present after `pull` |
| 11 | `! [rejected] ... (fetch first)` |

Step 11 is the lesson. Git **refuses** the push rather than quietly discarding the teammate's
commit. The hint it prints is the rule: *use 'git pull' before pushing again.*

// Your turn — retype the example above from memory, then run it.
// Typing beats reading. Peek above if you get stuck.

## `master` or `main`?

The session pushes to `master` throughout. This repository's branch is **`main`**.

| | |
|---|---|
| Older repos, and the session | `master` |
| GitHub's default since 2020 | `main` |
| How to check, always | `git branch --show-current` |

Copying `git push -u origin master` into a `main` repo gives
`error: src refspec master does not match any`. Check first.

// Your turn — retype the example above from memory, then run it.
// Typing beats reading. Peek above if you get stuck.

## Common mistakes

| Mistake | Symptom |
|---|---|
| Commit, then assume it is shared | nothing on GitHub; you never pushed |
| Push without pulling | `! [rejected] (fetch first)` |
| `git add .` from the wrong folder | half the project committed |
| `master` when the branch is `main` | `src refspec master does not match any` |
| Committing `node_modules/` | a huge, unreviewable repo - see [day3_3](/learn/w6/d3/p3) |

**Next:** [Day 3.3 - What a real repo does and never commits](/learn/w6/d3/p3)

parts.title: What a real repo does, and never commits

blocks.text:
# Week 6, Day 3.3 - What a real repo does, and never commits

Same commands, used the way a team uses them.

## The daily loop

```
git pull origin main        <- FIRST. before you write anything
...write tests...
git status                  <- read it; do not skip to add
git add -A
git commit -m "add payee validation tests"
git push origin main
```

Pull at the **start**, not just before pushing: you want to write against current code, not
discover a conflict an hour later.

## What never goes in

| Never commit | Why |
|---|---|
| `node_modules/` | thousands of files; `npm ci` rebuilds it exactly |
| `playwright-report/`, `test-results/` | regenerated every run; enormous diffs |
| **`.auth/` storage state** | a live session - [week5/day2_2](/learn/w5/d2/p2) |
| `.env`, credentials, tokens | history is forever, even after you delete the file |
| Visual baselines from another OS | platform-locked - [week4/day5_2](/learn/w4/d5/p2) |

That third row is the dangerous one. A storage-state file is a working credential, and a repo is
the easiest place in the world to leak one.

`git check-ignore -v` names the **line** that ignored it. That is how you prove a secret is safe
rather than hoping.

The file is gone and the token is not. Deleting a committed secret does **not** remove it - it is
in every clone and every fork. The only real fix is to **rotate the credential**.

## Commit messages a reviewer can use

| Poor | Better |
|---|---|
| `update` | `add payee validation tests` |
| `fix` | `fix flaky wait on transfer page` |
| `asdf` | `wire smoke suite into package.json` |

The session's `"adding new project"` is fine for a first commit. Six months later the only reason
anyone reads history is to answer *why did this change* - so answer it.

## Branches and pull requests

The session pushes straight to `master`. Real teams rarely do:

```
git checkout -b payee-tests     # your own branch
...commit...
git push -u origin payee-tests  # then open a Pull Request
```

| | Straight to main | Branch + PR |
|---|---|---|
| Review before it lands | no | **yes** |
| CI on the change alone | no | **yes** |
| Breaks everyone when wrong | **yes** | no |

This matters for Day 5: CI usually runs **on the pull request**, so a broken test is caught
before it reaches the branch everyone shares.

## Public or private

The session uses a public repo so anyone can clone it in Jenkins with no credentials. Convenient
for learning, wrong at work.

| | Public | Private |
|---|---|---|
| Jenkins needs credentials | no | **yes** |
| Your selectors, URLs, test data are visible | **to everyone** | to your team |

**Next:** [Day 3.4 - Practice](/learn/w6/d3/p4)

# Week 6, Day 3.4 - Practice

> **Do these in a scratch folder**, the way [day3_2](/learn/w6/d3/p2) does. Do not practise against

**Next:** [Day 4.1 - Prerequisites](/learn/w6/d4/p1)

problems.statement:
**Build one by hand**
Make a folder, `git init`, add a file, and get it to "committed" - reading `git status` after
every single command.

**Right when:** you can name what changed in `status` at each step, and `git log --oneline`
shows your commit.

**Your own local "GitHub"**
`git init --bare` a second folder, add it as `origin`, and push to it.

**Right when:** `git log` works inside the bare repo even though it holds no visible files - and
you can say why a server copy has none.

**Cause the rejection**
Clone your bare repo twice. Commit a different change to the same file in each. Push both.

**Right when:** the second push is rejected, and you can quote the hint git gives you.

**Resolve it**
Pull in the rejected clone and finish the job.

**Right when:** both changes are in `git log`, and you can say whether git merged them for you or
made you choose - and why.

**Prove a secret is ignored**
Create `.auth/fake.json` in your scratch repo, write a `.gitignore` that covers it, and prove it.

**Right when:** `git status` does not offer it **and** `git check-ignore -v` names the rule.

**Commit a secret, then try to remove it**
Commit a file with a fake token. Now delete the file and commit again.

**Right when:** you can still recover the token from `git log -p`, and you can say what that means
for a real leaked credential.

**Branch and merge**
Make a branch, commit on it, switch back to `master`, and merge.

**Right when:** `git log --oneline --graph` shows the shape, and you can explain why a team would
prefer this to committing on `master` directly.
